decisions.quote:
This exercise reproduces and assesses the historical time-series on the top shares of the wealth
distribution for the United States presented by Thomas Piketty in Capital in the Twenty-First
Century.
decisions.reason: Although the paper uses 'Replication' in its title, it does not collect new data or test the finding in a new sample; instead, it re-analyzes Piketty's publicly available spreadsheets, technical appendices, and underlying historical source series to reconstruct and evaluate his published U.S. wealth concentration series. Under the codebook, re-analyzing the original study's own data and calculations is a reproduction.

decisions.quote:
For 1980 Piketty reported that he averaged the 1983 figure from Wolff [1994] with the
1989 Federal Reserve figure from Kennickell [2009]. Had he done that, the number would be
67.7, but he reported 67.2 (which is the 1989 figure unaveraged). For 1990 Piketty’s spreadsheet
noted that he averaged three figures from “Kennickell 2001 Table 4” for the years 1992, 1995,
and 1998 [TS10.1DetailsUS]. But actually he used Kennickell [2009: Table 4, 35] [Piketty
2014b: 57]. The averaging procedure should have given him 67.8, but he reported 68.7,
probably a typo.
decisions.reason: Because the study type is a reproduction, the outcome must be coded on the two reproduction axes. On computation, following Piketty's stated averaging and adjustment procedures in his spreadsheets fails to recover several reported values due to calculation and spreadsheet errors ('computational issues'). On robustness, alternative and consistent constructions of the same underlying historical sources (such as applying the 1.2 household multiplier consistently to the 1870 top-10% estimate or avoiding arbitrary interpolations and constant 36-point markups) materially qualify or reverse the claimed historical trends ('robustness challenges').

decisions.quote: I replicate the figure from Science here as Figure 4. It reproduced the data in Figure 10.6 from Piketty’s book except it drops the point for 1810, but it now inexplicably adds a point for 1890 that isn't in the book’s version. The point plotted appears to be a simple linear interpolation between 1870 and 1910.
decisions.reason: Duplicate / secondary review article rather than an omitted target. Sutch explicitly describes Piketty and Saez (2014) in Science as 'a coauthored review with Emmanuel Saez which presents his data for the top ten percent' that 'reproduced the data in Figure 10.6 from Piketty’s book,' and Sutch's empirical critique in that section analyzes Piketty's book spreadsheet (TS10.1DetailsUS) and Technical Appendix (Piketty 2014b). Per the codebook rules on ruling out another work by the same authors and a review versus the primary study, it is not a separate original target.
